assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: RNA polymerase
items.clue: The enzyme that carries out transcription.

items.label: Elongation
items.clue: The stage of translation in which the polypeptide chain is lengthened.

items.label: Transfer RNA (tRNA)
items.clue: A small RNA molecule that carries a specific amino acid to the ribosome.

items.label: Codon
items.clue: A sequence of three bases on an mRNA molecule that specifies one amino acid, or signals the start or stop of translation.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the roles of RNA polymerase in transcription?

options.text: It separates the DNA strands and links RNA nucleotides, positioned by pairing with the template strand, into one RNA strand.
It links RNA nucleotides into a strand once helicase has opened the DNA and a primer has been laid down.
It copies both DNA strands of the gene at the same time, producing a double-stranded RNA molecule from the gene.
It joins amino acids together, one after another, in the order specified by the base sequence of the gene.

questions.stem: A section of the DNA template strand of a gene has the base sequence TACGCAT. What is the base sequence of the RNA transcribed from this section?

options.text: UACGCAU
AUGCGUA
UAGCGAU
ATGCGTA

questions.explanation: Each RNA base is complementary to the template base opposite it: T pairs with A, A on the template pairs with U, C with G and G with C, giving AUGCGUA.

options.text: A base sequence of DNA is used as a template to make a complementary mRNA molecule inside the cell nucleus.
Ribosomes convert the bases of the mRNA into amino acids, which are then joined into a chain.
The base sequence of an mRNA molecule is used to determine the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide.
Amino acids are joined into a polypeptide inside the nucleus, right beside the DNA of the gene that codes for it.

questions.stem: Which statement about the binding of mRNA and tRNA to a ribosome is correct?

options.text: The mRNA binds to the large subunit, because it is the larger molecule, and the tRNAs bind to the small subunit.
The mRNA binds to the small subunit, and only one tRNA can bind to the large subunit at any moment.
The mRNA binds to the small subunit, and every tRNA needed for the polypeptide binds along it at once.
The mRNA binds to the small subunit, and two tRNAs can bind to the large subunit at the same time.

questions.stem: The start codon on an mRNA molecule is AUG. Which tRNA anticodon binds to this codon, and how is it held there?

options.text: AUG, the same three bases as the codon
UAC, held to the codon by hydrogen bonds
TAC, with thymine pairing to adenine
UAC, bonded to the codon by covalent bonds

questions.explanation: The anticodon is complementary to the codon: A pairs with U, U with A and G with C, giving UAC. The codon and anticodon are held together by hydrogen bonds, which break when the tRNA leaves.

questions.stem: Why does the genetic code use codons of three bases rather than two?

options.text: Two bases would give 16 codons, which is close enough to 20 for nearly all the amino acids to be coded.
Three bases allow each codon to code for up to three different amino acids whenever these are needed.
Three bases give 64 possible codons, enough for 20 amino acids, whereas two bases give only 16.
Three bases let the ribosome start reading at any point, since any group of three is a codon.

questions.stem: An mRNA molecule has the base sequence AUGUUUGCUUAAGGC, read from the first base. The genetic code table gives: AUG methionine (start), UUU phenylalanine, GCU alanine, UAA stop, GGC glycine. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide translated from it?

options.text: two amino acids
four amino acids
three amino acids
fifteen amino acids

questions.stem: How is the polypeptide chain lengthened during translation?

options.text: All the tRNAs first line up along the whole length of the mRNA, and their amino acids are then joined together in one step.
Each tRNA stays attached to its own amino acid, so the chain is a series of tRNAs joined through their amino acids.
Each new amino acid is held to the previous one by hydrogen bonds, like those between codon and anticodon.
The ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon at a time, and a peptide bond links each new amino acid to the chain.

questions.stem: A base substitution in a gene changes an mRNA codon from GGU to GGC. Both codons code for glycine. What is the effect on the polypeptide?

options.text: Its structure changes, because a different codon is bound to give a different amino acid.
Every amino acid after this point changes, because the reading frame has been shifted.
There is no effect, because the same amino acid, glycine, is inserted at that position.
Glycine may be replaced, because GGC can also code for a different amino acid.

questions.stem: A cell contains many different kinds of tRNA molecule. What is the role of a tRNA during translation?

options.text: It brings a specific amino acid to the ribosome and pairs its anticodon with the matching codon on the mRNA.
It binds to a codon first and then collects from the cytoplasm whichever amino acid that codon specifies.
It delivers an amino acid and remains bonded to it, becoming part of the finished polypeptide chain.
It carries the mRNA bases that the ribosome converts into the amino acids of the polypeptide.

questions.stem: The genetic code is described as degenerate. What does this mean?

options.text: A single codon can code for two or more different amino acids.
The same codons code for the same amino acids in all organisms.
Some amino acids are coded for by two bases and some by three bases.
Most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon.

questions.explanation: Degeneracy means that several codons can specify the same amino acid: 61 codons code for 20 amino acids, so for example GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG all code for glycine.

questions.stem: Which statement about the direction of translation is correct?

options.text: The ribosome can begin at either end of the mRNA, since the start codon is recognized wherever it is met.
The ribosome moves along the mRNA from its 5' end towards its 3' end, so the codon nearest the 5' end is translated first.
The ribosome moves along the mRNA from its 3' end towards its 5' end, matching the direction the template is read.
The ribosome begins at the 5' cap and translates every base up to and including the poly-A tail at the 3' end.

questions.stem: Which statement about non-coding sequences in eukaryotic DNA is correct?

options.text: Non-coding sequences such as introns and telomeres have no function at all and so are never transcribed into RNA.
Every gene codes for a polypeptide, so tRNA and rRNA are both produced by translation of their own mRNA molecules.
The promoter of a gene is transcribed and forms the first codons of the mRNA for that gene.
The genes for tRNA and rRNA are transcribed, but their RNA products are never translated into polypeptides.

questions.stem: What is the role of the 5' cap and the 3' poly-A tail added to a eukaryotic mRNA transcript?

options.text: They are translated, adding a short run of extra amino acids to each end of the polypeptide.
They stabilize the mRNA, protecting it from being broken down before it is translated.
They mark the positions of the introns so that the splicing enzymes know which sections to remove.
They have no function, being left over from transcription of non-coding DNA at each end of the gene.

questions.stem: Which sequence of events initiates translation of an mRNA in a eukaryotic cell?

options.text: The complete ribosome binds directly to the start codon as a single unit, and the initiator tRNA then enters the ribosome and pairs with the codon.
The small subunit binds to the 3' end of the mRNA and moves along until it reaches the start codon, where the large subunit attaches.
The small subunit binds at the start codon, and the initiator tRNA enters at the E site before the large subunit attaches to it.
The small subunit binds to the 5' end of the mRNA and moves to the start codon; the initiator tRNA binds there; then the large subunit attaches.

questions.stem: Why does a cell continually break down some of its proteins in proteasomes while synthesizing new ones?

options.text: Proteins are permanent once they have been made, so proteasomes act only when a cell has been badly damaged or is about to die.
Proteasomes break down proteins only when the cell is short of glucose and needs amino acids as a source of energy.
Sustaining a functional proteome needs constant turnover: proteins no longer needed are removed and their amino acids reused.
The amino acids released by proteasomes are waste products that the cell must excrete, so breakdown removes unwanted material.
